Recovered property

One laptop, no owner.

This laptop was left behind at the Driftwood Café on the morning of Friday, October 16 — tucked beside a cold oat latte, still warm, still logged in. The owner never came back for it.

Four days later, nobody has heard from Nadia Ruiz, 28 — marine biology grad student, whale photographer, owner of one extremely smug cat. Her roommate has the laptop now, and one question:

Where is Nadia? Everything she left behind is on this machine. Emails, texts, photos, files. Snoop carefully.

Case closed

She was never missing. She was at sea.

On Wednesday, October 14, Nadia's advisor quietly put her name on a waitlist. On Thursday, a researcher dropped out of the Pacific Cetacean Institute's fall survey, and Dr. Ellison offered Nadia the berth — ten days aboard the R/V Aurora, tracking sperm whales, under a strict no-personal-devices protocol.

She said yes in under thirty minutes. She packed one dry bag, arranged for June to feed Miso, told almost no one (her mother would have spent ten days imagining pirate attacks), and was at Pier 9 by 5:40 AM on Friday — stopping only for one coffee she never finished, and leaving one laptop she absolutely meant to come back for.

The sinister texts from "K."? Kai Tanaka, the Aurora's first mate, confirming her berthing time. The fight with Sam? An ex, being an ex — he texted her "go catch your whales" before she'd even boarded. The terrifying deleted draft? Read to the end: it was joy, badly previewed.

The Aurora docks at Pier 9 on Sunday, October 25, around 4 PM. Nadia is fine. She's probably seen more whales this week than most people see in a lifetime.

Epilogue — found in Case Notes, dated Oct 25, 7:12 PM:

"Okay. Whoever you are: you cracked my folder password, read my drafts, AND solved me. Terrifying. Impressive. The café gave the laptop back today. For the record — I saw eleven sperm whales and one very rude albatross. Worth it. — N"
